what_its_for: Zolpidem helps you fall asleep and stay asleep if you have trouble sleeping (insomnia). It works by calming your brain so you can get a good night's rest. It is meant for short-term use only, usually no longer than 1 to 2 weeks.
how_to_take: Take zolpidem by mouth right before you get into bed. Only take it when you have at least 7 to 8 full hours available to sleep before you need to wake up. Do not take it with or right after a meal, as food can slow down how fast it works. Swallow regular tablets whole. If you have the extended-release tablet (Ambien CR), swallow it whole — do not crush, chew, or split it. The sublingual tablet (Edluar or Intermezzo) goes under your tongue and dissolves — do not swallow it whole.
dosing: Your doctor will choose the right dose for you. The usual starting dose for adults is 5 mg for women and either 5 mg or 10 mg for men, taken once per night. Women and older adults are often given lower doses because the medicine stays in the body longer. Never take more than your doctor prescribed, and never take more than one dose in a single night.
missed_dose: Zolpidem is taken only when you need it for sleep, not on a fixed daily schedule. If you forget to take it but you still have at least 7 to 8 hours before you need to wake up, you can take it then. If you are already close to your wake-up time, skip it entirely. Never double up or take two doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store zolpidem at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, light, and moisture — so the bathroom cabinet is not a good spot. Keep it in a secure location out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medication down the toilet; ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program near you.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking zolpidem — it can cause extreme drowsiness, breathing problems, and even be life-threatening. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be fully alert the morning after taking it, because the medicine can still be in your system. Avoid taking other sleep aids, anxiety medicines, pain medications, muscle relaxers, or antihistamines (like Benadryl) unless your doctor says it is okay. Do not take zolpidem if you cannot get a full night's sleep.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sleepwalking, sleep-driving, or doing other activities while asleep that you do not remember (like cooking or eating); unusual thoughts or behaviors; memory problems or confusion the next day; feeling depressed or having thoughts of harming yourself; an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing; or if your sleep problems get worse or do not improve after 7 to 10 days of use.
when_it_works: Zolpidem works quickly — usually within 15 to 30 minutes of taking it. That is why you should only take it when you are ready to go to sleep right away. The extended-release form (Ambien CR) is designed to help you both fall asleep and stay asleep throughout the night.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and older): You will likely be given a lower dose (5 mg) because this medicine stays in your body longer and increases your risk of falls, dizziness, and confusion. Get up slowly from bed. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Talk to your doctor before taking zolpidem. It can pass into breast milk and may cause drowsiness in a nursing baby. People with liver problems: Your doctor may lower your dose since your body may process the medicine more slowly. Children and teenagers: Zolpidem is not approved for use in anyone under 18 years old.
